episode_title: AI, Data, and Circular Design: Rethinking Architecture's Material Future with Christopher Bamborough

real_qa.q: How can architects collaborate with AI rather than simply use it as task automation?
real_qa.r: Collaboration requires a feedback loop where the human applies aesthetic, political, and economic lenses to AI outputs rather than accepting frictionless pathways to outcomes. Most presentations treat AI as offloading tasks with image generation software that produces one endpoint result without critical engagement on whether it achieves design goals. True collaboration means the feedback loop comes from the human rather than just sloppy AI-generated results.

real_qa.q: What is circular design in architecture and how does AI support material reuse?
real_qa.r: Circularity anticipates a future where material extraction cannot be relied upon, moving beyond the 15-year focus on sustainability and recent decarbonisation emphasis. The big problem in reusing materials is keeping track of all of them, which is fundamentally a data management problem that AI is the best solution for. Circularity requires tracking material flows and enabling reuse rather than continuous extraction.
real_qa.requete: circular design AI material reuse tracking

real_qa.q: Why did Zaha Hadid Architects train their own LLM instead of using ChatGPT?
real_qa.r: ZHA (formerly Zaha Hadid Architects) trained their own AI because they have so many buildings in their back catalog documented through images and data. By training a ZHA-specific LLM instead of dealing with the general ChatGPT LLM, they can be much more specific about requirements, define input and output parameters, and produce 50 versions that maintain Zaha Hadid's particular design aesthetic and look-and-feel for architects to choose from.
real_qa.requete: Zaha Hadid Architects custom LLM training

real_qa.q: How does authorship and creativity change when architects use LLMs for image generation?
real_qa.r: Authorship becomes diluted when using LLMs because there is a space of generation you do not really control. The LLM is trained on a large body of images without knowing whether designs are good or not, so even in a collaboration, your authorship is lost while its authorship is based on creative work previously produced by architects and photographers. This creates a perverse relationship where we lose authorship while the LLM's outputs rely entirely on what we previously created.

real_qa.q: What is the historical understanding of data in architecture and how does it introduce bias?
real_qa.r: Data is not something simply given through science or technology but rather captured for specific cultural reasons. It is essentially a selection of evidence that fits a worldview or argument, and even machine sensor data collected by particular technology for particular reasons produces particular conclusions. In architecture practice, data-driven design requires questioning what data is being used, where it comes from, and why it was chosen, because there is always a slight bias in how data is collected and applied to decisions.
real_qa.requete: data bias architecture cultural selection evidence

guest.bio_context: Christopher Bamborough trained as an architect in the UK and Australia, worked in architectural practice in London and Sydney, and specialized in digital design and digital fabrication around 2011-2012. He later pivoted to teaching computational design and coding skills at universities including University of Sydney and UTS, and is now conducting postdoctoral research at UNSW exploring how data, digital fabrication, and intelligent systems reshape architecture, sustainability, and the role of the architect.
